title: Fast & Slow Pointers
description: Use two pointers moving at different speeds to detect cycles, middle positions, and distance gaps.
identify: The list may contain a cycle.
You need to find a middle, loop start, or remove a node from the end.
A fixed gap between two pointers can avoid measuring the full list twice.
The solution should use O(1) extra space.
explanation: Fast and slow pointers exploit relative speed. If a cycle exists, the faster pointer must eventually meet the slower pointer. If a fixed distance is needed, one pointer can be advanced first and both can move together.

title: Reverse
description: Change next pointers carefully while preserving access to the remaining list.
identify: The problem asks to reverse a list, sublist, or fixed-size group.
Node links must be rewired in-place.
You need to remember previous, current, and next nodes.
Carry or arithmetic can be done while traversing reversed order.
explanation: Reversal is pointer bookkeeping. Before changing curr->next, store the next node. Then point curr backward, move prev forward, and continue.

title: Dummy Nodes
description: Use a sentinel node to simplify head changes, merges, partitions, and list construction.
identify: The head node may change.
You are building a new linked-list order from existing nodes.
Multiple edge cases appear around the first node.
A tail pointer can append nodes cleanly.
explanation: A dummy node removes special handling for the first inserted node. Build from dummy.next and keep tail at the last node of the result.

title: Special
description: Handle linked-list problems that need extra mapping, pointer identity, or intersection reasoning.
identify: Nodes have extra pointers such as random pointers.
The answer depends on node identity, not just node value.
Two lists may physically share nodes.
A hash map or clever pointer switching can preserve O(N) time.
explanation: Special linked-list problems often require preserving node identity. Hash maps are direct and safe; pointer-switching can solve intersection without extra space.

title: K-way Merge
description: Merge many sorted linked lists using a priority queue or divide-and-conquer.
identify: There are multiple sorted linked lists.
You repeatedly need the smallest current head.
The total number of nodes is large compared with the number of lists.
A min-heap can reduce repeated scans.
explanation: A min-heap keeps the smallest head among k lists available in O(log k). Each node enters and leaves the heap once.
